name: PT Bayan Resources Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Bayan Resources: a first-quartile thermal producer on the wrong side of the konglo premium
frontmatter.summary: A low-cost, net-cash, high-payout thermal-coal pure play whose fundamentals support far less than the tape. Re-run through the konglo lens: the life-of-asset value is Rp4,265 a share against a price of Rp10,475, and the regime deck's most-likely path keeps only part of that premium over twelve months — a target of Rp7,909, REDUCE, total return -19.3%.
thesis: Fundamentals first: a full life-of-asset DCF at the deck's long-run Newcastle marker, with no terminal value, supports a fundamental twelve-month value of Rp4,265 a share against Rp10,475 traded — the coal does not pay for the price [S0].

The price is a konglo premium rather than a coal value: the shares trade at 2.4x the fundamental value, and for a name on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list the engine's konglo lens sets the most likely twelve-month price from the regime deck rather than assume instant convergence [S19].
Under that lens the base regime closes only part of the gap — the target is Rp7,909 — and the bear regime, where the de-rating runs at a second shock-year pace, takes it to Rp5,313 [S17].

The franchise itself is genuinely good — first-quartile cash costs, a net-cash balance sheet and a long reserve life — which is why we are cautious rather than negative on the asset, only on the entry price [S6, S8].

The pending change of control is both the governance flag and a dated price catalyst: a conditional agreement would hand the control block to PT Jhonlin Baratama and, on completion, the takeover rules would require a mandatory tender offer that sets a floor under the exit [S2, S10].

blocks.text: This is an update that re-runs the published view through the house konglo lens, and it changes the arithmetic of the conclusion rather than its direction. Bayan is a member of Low Tuck Kwong's group and sits on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list [S19], so the engine values it on the fundamentals first and then sets the most likely twelve-month price from the konglo regime deck: the fundamental twelve-month value is Rp4,265 a share, the shares trade at 2.4x that value, and the lens keeps only part of the premium over the year ahead, which gives a target of Rp7,909. Most of the fundamental work is as before — the licence and royalty basis, the real-terms unit costs and the re-mirrored business scenarios [S6, S8]. Two things moved in this revision, both in the same direction and both sourced: the base volume now follows the company's own plan and funded capacity rather than sitting below it [S6, F47, S13], and the reserve is netted for the tonnes mined since the last JORC statement instead of being left to the tail [S6, S7]. Together they raise the fundamental value modestly and change the arithmetic, not the direction. What changed most is that our target no longer assumes the premium vanishes on day one; the regime deck says how much of it the most likely path still keeps.

We move our coverage of Bayan Resources to REDUCE with a twelve-month target of Rp7,909, implying a total return of -19.3% from the last close of Rp10,475 [S0]. The company is an unusually clean thermal-coal producer: it mines low-cost sub-bituminous coal in East and South Kalimantan, sells a quarter of its tonnes into the Indonesian domestic market, and has run a net-cash balance sheet with a five-year average payout of 73.0% of profit [S6, S8]. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the price the market now pays for it.

Our primary method is a life-of-asset discounted cash flow that runs over the stated JORC reserve base and stops when the coal is mined out, with no terminal value [S9]. Struck at the sector deck's through-cycle Newcastle marker, and with the realisation haircut the method card requires of an Indonesian producer selling below the Australian marker, it supports Rp4,191 a share [S0]. Blended with the cross-checks, rolled forward a year at the cost of equity and net of the next twelve months' dividend, that becomes the fundamental twelve-month value of Rp4,265 a share — well below the traded price, and the single most important number in this report. The two cross-checks we use to stress it now part company: the exit-multiple cross-check lands close to the reserve DCF, while the dividend-yield anchor sits far above both — and all three sit below the price, which is what section four explains.

The market, in our reading, is not valuing the reserve life at all. It is valuing a dividend stream at a very low yield and a benchmark that reflects a war premium rather than a marginal-cost floor [S0]. Our reverse-DCF work says the current price requires the benchmark to hold near US$191/t through the forecast horizon, a level above even the current premium spot rather than the deck's long-run path [S0]. We are therefore cautious on the entry price, not on the company. The gap between what the tape implies and what the reserve is worth is the konglo premium the regime deck prices; section four shows why we expect the most likely path to keep part of it for another year rather than close it at once, and section five sets the regime scenarios that decide how much.

Thermal coal is the workhorse fuel of Asian electricity generation, and Indonesia is the largest
seaborne exporter of it. Producers in the region sell on a mix of index-linked and fixed-price
contracts, with domestic obligations layered on top of export sales. Prices are set globally but
realisations differ by calorific value, ash and sulphur content, and by distance to the importing
market.

Bayan Resources is a thermal-coal producer with mining and infrastructure operations concentrated in Kalimantan, Indonesia [S6]. The group sells unwashed and washed thermal coal and operates its own hauling, barging and port-loading chain, which is unusual among Indonesian producers and is central to its cost position [S8]. In the most recent full year the company produced 68.0 Mt and sold 70.8 Mt of coal, a record for the group and a function of both a large-volume year and the drawdown of stockpiles built in the prior period [S6].

The revenue model is a single dominant line — thermal coal — with a small non-coal tail in plantations and services that is immaterial to group value [S6]. Because the company reports in US dollars, its revenue and costs are largely currency-matched: coal is sold in dollars and the bulk of its mining, hauling and barging inputs are contracted in dollars or in rupiah at rates that reprice slowly [S8]. That natural hedge is a genuine advantage for a producer whose costs are domestic and whose revenues are export-linked [S8].

The realised price is the swing variable in the model. Bayan's product is lower-calorific-value sub-bituminous coal: the company disclosed that 67.2 Mt was committed for the current year at an average calorific value of 4,088 kcal/kg GAR [S8], roughly a third below the 6,000 kcal/kg NAR benchmark the Newcastle marker is priced at, and consistent with the method card's prescription that an Indonesian producer realises off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle. The modelled long-run realisation ratio of 45% of the Newcastle marker is the arithmetic of that grade discount and the DMO-capped domestic share, calibrated back through the reported realisations of US$48.4/t and US$61.3/t [S6, S8]. The ratio is corroborated by the sector deck's own government prints rather than asserted: HBA II at 4,100 kcal/kg GAR — the grade Bayan's book sits on — clears at US$66.1/t against a Newcastle spot of US$150/t, a ratio essentially equal to ours, whereas the covered peer AADI realises far less of a discount because its ultra-low-pollutant Envirocoal clears at a higher calorific value and so nearer the HBA I level, around US$93.6/t [S0, S8]. The gap to the peer is grade, not company execution. Structurally, the discount is a function of coal quality and the tax regime rather than of company execution [S6]. Management's own framing of the last two years is instructive: a large volume gain and a materially lower average selling price of US$48.4/t, a combination that shows how much of the earnings line is benchmark rather than operating [S6].

The domestic leg of the business is a structural feature rather than an afterthought. Roughly 25.7% of tonnes went to Indonesian buyers in the last full year, which places that share of volume under the domestic market obligation regime and its price cap [S6]. The company meets part of that obligation in kind from its lower-cost operations and pays compensation on other volumes, so the economic effect of the cap is diluted but not eliminated [S8]. In the bull scenario it is precisely the domestic share that stops realisations rising as fast as the export marker [S0].

On market position, Bayan is a top-tier Indonesian exporter by volume but not the largest, and its distinctive claim is cost rather than scale [S6]. The company describes its Tabang operations as among the lowest-cost thermal coal mines in the country, and the group-level strip ratio of 4.5x is low for the basin [S6, S8]. Group structure is a holding company over a set of operating subsidiaries, and the controlling shareholder position is currently in flux following a block transfer that section six covers in detail [S2, S10].

Strategy, as the company frames it, is volume growth funded from internally generated cash, continued investment in the Muara Pahu and Tabang barge-loading capacity, and a high dividend payout rather than balance-sheet expansion [S6, S8]. Capex guidance for the current year of a two-to-three hundred million dollar range, against a depreciation charge that is small next to EBITDA, tells the same story: the fleet and the logistics are largely contracted and expensed, so the business converts a large share of EBITDA into cash [S0, S6].

Indonesian thermal coal is an export industry with a domestic obligation grafted on top, and both halves matter to a name like Bayan [S6]. The seaborne market is priced off the Australian and South African markers, but an Indonesian producer's realisation is set by its own calorific value, its ash and sulphur content, the freight differential to the importing market and the tax regime [S6]. The method card is explicit on this point: Indonesian coal names key off the domestic and Indonesian-export indices rather than the Australian marker, and any model that prices them off Newcastle at face value will overstate their revenue [S8].

The demand side is Asia, and increasingly India and South-East Asia rather than China alone [S6]. Chinese policy on domestic mine safety and output, Indian import appetite and the pace of new coal-fired capacity in South-East Asia set the level around which prices oscillate [S6]. Supply is the more interesting half: Indonesian output is administratively gated through the RKAB approval regime, which sets the permitted production plan for each operating entity [S13]. That gate is binding in practice, not in theory — as the current year demonstrated when three Bayan subsidiaries were unable to produce legally pending an approval and declared force majeure to their customers [S13].

The regulatory layer is where the industry-specific risk sits. The domestic market obligation requires producers to supply a share of output to the domestic power market, and the price at which those tonnes are sold has historically been capped well below the export benchmark [S6]. Alongside it, the royalty regime for coal was reworked through the 2025 regulations, and coal royalties now run on two tracks. Producers who took their licences into the new permit form face a stepped, price-linked schedule [S0]. Bayan sits on the contract track: the annual report discloses that the group mines through 5 coal contracts of work, or CCoW, and further IUP licences held by its subsidiaries, and the CCoW note states the Government is entitled to take 13.5% of the coal produced from those five legacy mines, while the IUP licences pay a stepped production fee whose top rate is 11.5% by calorific value and reference-price tier [S6]. What the accounts actually book is the blend of the two — a royalty and production-fee expense of US$269.1m in the last full year and US$263.8m the year before — which is why we model a single flat effective rate rather than either headline [S6].

Competitive positioning within the basin is a cost question first and a scale question second [S6]. Bayan's group strip ratio of 4.5x is well inside the Kalimantan norm, and its self-operated hauling and barging chain removes a layer of contractor margin that most peers pay [S8]. The company's own history of low cash costs — US$32.5/t in the last full year against a budget of a materially higher figure — is evidence that the advantage is operational rather than cyclical [S6]. On a cost-curve basis we would place the group in the first quartile of Indonesian thermal producers, which is the moat the method card asks us to identify [S6, S8].

Five-forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate and rising, because fuel, labour and contracting rates set the cost line and the company named higher fuel prices as the principal driver of its recent cost increase [S8]. Buyer power is low in the export market and high in the domestic market, because the latter is a regulated monopsony [S6]. Substitutes are the long-run threat to thermal coal, and the energy transition is a structural headwind rather than a near-term one [S6]. Rivalry is intense and commoditised, with no pricing power at the individual producer level [S6]. Entry is gated by the licence regime, which cuts both ways: it protects incumbents and it handed three Bayan subsidiaries a production stoppage in the current year [S13].

Our industry complex view, consistent with the desk's neutral stance on thermal coal, is that the observed spot benchmark embeds a war premium that the deck mean-reverts over its forecast horizon [S0]. That is the single assumption that drives most of our valuation gap, and the sensitivity grid in section four shows how the answer moves with it [S0].

Coal-fired generation remains the largest single source of electricity in much of Asia, and
retirements in developed markets have been more than offset by additions in emerging ones. Exporters
compete on delivered cost, and freight, calorific value and ash content decide whether a cargo is
economic in a given market. Governments influence the industry through permitting, royalty regimes
and domestic-supply obligations rather than through direct ownership.

The historical record is one of a high-margin, cash-generative business whose earnings are set by the benchmark rather than by operating leverage. In the last full year the group reported revenue of US$3,427.6m and a net profit to parent of US$767.9m [S0], and the company's own annual report discloses EBITDA of US$1,160.0m on that year [S6]. Our engine models EBITDA of US$1,113.4m — an EBITDA margin of 32.5% — a figure that differs from the disclosed one by a few percent and traces to the depreciation basis rather than to any operating line, since the data pack's D&A for this name is a stub (section below). The prior year was broadly similar at the revenue line, which is the point: volume grew sharply while the realised price fell, so revenue was almost exactly flat year on year [S0, S6].

The cost side is the franchise. Cash costs per tonne came down to US$32.5/t, comfortably inside the prior year's US$37.8/t and well inside the budget for both years [S6, S7]. Our forecast carries that advantage forward rather than fading it, because the drivers are structural — a low strip ratio, the self-operated logistics chain and a weak regional cost base [S6, S8]. The model's unit cost is built bottom-up from the mining block, the hauling and barging block and a royalty line, at a single effective royalty rate of 8% of revenue reconciled to the Company's own disclosed cost stack, where the royalty share of the all-in quarterly cash cost implies under a tenth of revenue at the reported quarterly ASP, against the two full-year histories either side of it [S8, F5, F6]. That reported cost already includes royalty, so the mining blocks are carried ex-royalty and the line is counted once, not twice. On peer comparability, a caveat the cost block requires: unlike some covered coal names we carry a per-tonne cost intensity rather than a physical bcm/t strip ratio in the model, so the 4.5x group strip ratio is context, not the cost driver the multiple axis turns on. The quantity that is comparable across the peer set is the per-tonne cash cost, and on that basis Bayan's mining block sits at or below the covered names once its self-operated hauling and barging chain is allowed for [S8, F7]. On the royalty itself we book the effective rate, not a headline: the group mines under coal contracts of work, or CCoW, as well as IUP licences [S6, F28], the CCoW contract rate is 13.5% and the IUP production fee steps up to 11.5% [S6], but the consolidated royalty and production-fee expense the accounts actually show is US$269.1m against US$3,427.6m of revenue in the last full year and US$263.8m the year before — so the flat 8% of revenue in the model carries the blend the company pays, not the contract ceiling, and the licence base is now stated rather than inferred [S6]. Benchmarked against the covered peer set the effective rate looks low — AADI, an IUPK continuation-of-contract holder on the stepped schedule, books a materially higher rate — but the gap is the LICENCE rather than the assumption: Bayan's coal-contract-of-work royalty is contract-specific, so it sits below the IUPK band, and the IUP/CCoW-conversion step-up toward the 11.5% top IUP rate is carried explicitly in the bear rather than assumed away [S6, F28, F30].

Our forecast volumes follow the company's own plan and funded capacity rather than sitting below it. Management is targeting FY2026 coal production at the higher end of its guided range — 76.0 Mt [S6, F47] — and is ramping Tabang toward its stated 80 million-tonne-per-annum capacity on the 770 USD m already spent [S6, F33], so the model lifts from 73.0 Mt in FY2026E into 80.0 Mt by FY2028E and holds it flat thereafter rather than fading it: the stated JORC reserve base of 2,030 Mt, dated 1 April 2022 and the company's latest statement, supports roughly two and a half decades at this run-rate, so nothing in the reserve statement or the contracted book sources a decline, and we do not put an unsourced one in [S6, S8]. FY2026E sits just below the top of the guided range rather than at it because 1H26 sales of 32.2 Mt ran flat year on year and the September force-majeure halt by three subsidiaries clips the second half [S8, S13]; the 67.2 Mt committed book is a floor to the volume line, not the plan [S8].

Our current-year revenue and profit run above the company's own FY2026 plan, and the gap needs reconciling because it is the price deck rather than the operating plan. Bayan's own FY2026 plan assumes a Newcastle price of 105.0 USD/t and, on that assumption, guides revenue to US$1.8bn to US$3.8bn and EBITDA of US$0.5bn to US$1.0bn [S6]. We carry the group volume inside the guided production range — modelled FY2026E sales of 73.0 Mt — but price it off the sector deck's FY2026E Newcastle marker of US$137/t [S0], which sits above the company's own planning price, so modelled FY2026E revenue of US$4,485.4m and EBITDA of US$1,911.3m land above the top of the guided band. Held at the company's own price plan the forecast would fall back toward it: the difference is the deck's near-year marker, which the method card re-sets whenever the complex moves, not a divergence from the operating plan on volume or cost.

Cash conversion is excellent and is the reason the dividend is credible. Operating cash flow in the last full year was US$501.4m before working-capital swings and capex, capex was US$170.9m, and the balance sheet ended with net debt of US$-574.6m [S0]. That is a genuine negative net-debt figure, not a rounding artefact, and it means the group's net-debt-to-EBITDA is negative in a trough as well as in a peak [S0]. A producer with no leverage and a first-quartile cost position can survive a severe price fall that would force a levered peer into a distressed equity raise, which is exactly the asymmetry the method card wants us to price [S0, S8].

Both the da key and the D&A charge itself are restated from the LK notes rather than the data pack (fixed-asset depreciation of US$111.1m in FY2025 and US$96.6m in FY2024 [S6], sourced in the segment note; the data pack reads under three million). That restatement lifts reported history EBITDA from the pack's understated figure to the one the table shows, because the pack's D&A line is the stub — not the charge. Capital allocation is the clearest signal of management's intent. The company paid US$500 of dividends in respect of the last completed year against a five-year average payout of 73.0%, and it has done so while funding its capacity programme internally [S8]. We model the payout at 73%, held broadly flat, which is a genuine judgement: a lower benchmark with an unchanged payout ratio would cut the dividend materially, and that is the transmission channel between the coal price and the share price [S0, S8].

Earnings quality. We have worked through the methodology's flag list and the picture is unusually clean for the sector. On accruals, the divergence between accounting profit and cash generation is small and stable, with capex and depreciation both low relative to EBITDA and no evidence of capitalised costs masking a cash shortfall [S0]. The related-party screen is not entirely clean, and we state it as we find it, quantified. The group's coal revenue includes a related-party slice of US$185.9m in the last full year, a low-single-digit share of group sales [S6]. The related-party balance sheet is larger than the revenue flow: trade payables to related parties were US$35.2m and trade receivables from them US$12.3m at the last balance-sheet date, and there is a related-party civil-works contract with PT Nirmala Matranusa (NMN) for the Senyiur jetty worth US$51.9m across the 2023-24 fiscal years [S6]. On the accrual screen the picture is the opposite of an aggressive one: the group's operating cash generation exceeds its reported profit, so the accruals ratio is negative — cash is running ahead of accounting earnings rather than behind them — and we find no receivable or inventory build that outruns revenue [S0]. Our verdict is optics-class, not manipulation-class: the flows are disclosed line by line, small against revenue and assets, and the coal is also sold to third-party customers — but the related-party payable is not nothing, and it sits beside the off-market block transfer that section six discusses rather than being waved away [S6]. There is no serial equity issuance, no pledge disclosure of the kind that would impair control, and no auditor downgrade or qualified opinion in the covered period [S6].

Two flags do need stating. First, the group's working-capital position and its receivables profile warrant monitoring, because a producer selling into a regulated domestic market carries a payment-timing risk that export-only peers do not [S0, S6]. Second, the effective royalty and tax lines are policy variables rather than operating ones, and the 2025 coal regulations introduced a stepped royalty schedule that could raise the cost line for producers in the converted-licence regime [S0]. Bayan states it sits outside that regime, but it is a live policy risk and we treat it as such in section five [S8]. Finally, the off-market block transfer that section six discusses is a governance flag rather than an accounting one, and we flag it here because it bears on how an investor should weight the reported earnings stream [S2].

Reported profit for a coal producer is a poor guide to the value of the business, because the price
that produced it will not persist. The cash-conversion question is the important one: how much of
each dollar of earnings survives as free cash after capex and working capital, and how much of that
is returned. A producer that converts earnings into cash and returns it to shareholders is worth
more than the same earnings stream retained in a business with no reinvestment opportunity.

We value Bayan with a life-of-asset discounted cash flow as the primary method, weighted 60% of the target, with an exit-multiple cross-check at 25% and a dividend-yield cross-check at 15% [S0]. The method set fits the industry because the asset is a depleting reserve with a finite life, not a growth business: the method card is explicit that a cyclical producer should never be valued on a single year's earnings, and that the correct frame is the net present value of the cash the reserve will generate at a through-cycle price, less debt and corporate costs [S0, S9].

We build the discount rate from the macro deck rather than from feel. The risk-free rate is 5.0% in dollar terms, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, and the Indonesian country risk premium adds 2.5%, giving a cost of equity of 11.3% [S0]. We take the equity beta from the industry regression rather than from a subjective judgement, and because the company carries no net debt the gearing adjustment is nil, so the weighted average cost of capital equals the cost of equity at 11.3% [S0]. On top of the regression beta we carry a governance overhang in the base case itself, not only in the bear: a live exchange clarification over the off-market control-block transfer at Rp2,588 against a tape near Rp11,100 [S2, S10] and a September force-majeure stoppage that was outside minority control [S13] justify a small required-return overlay, which is why our cost of equity sits inside rather than below the covered coal peer range. We assume no terminal growth at all, which is deliberate: a depleting thermal-coal asset should not be assigned perpetual real growth, so the value sits in the explicit cash flows rather than in a terminal multiple [S0].

The primary DCF runs on the company's latest published JORC reserve statement, 2,030 Mt, dated 1 April 2022 and still shown on its Reserve & Resources page [S9, S11] — but NETS the tonnes physically mined out of it since. That netting is a base-case adjustment, not a haircut, and we apply it here rather than leave it to the bear: disclosed production of 56.2 Mt in FY2024 and 68.0 Mt in FY2025, on top of a similar FY2023, has removed roughly two hundred million tonnes of the reserve since the statement date [S6, S7], so the reserve the mine plan actually has left is nearer two and a half decades than three, and the base DCF runs a twenty-five-year horizon to FY2050E — the last producing year — rather than into empty tail years of sustaining capex and no revenue. The headline 2,030 Mt is the company's latest statement and we do not invent a replacement; if a newer JORC statement is published the horizon, and with it the DCF value, moves with it, and we will re-strike it then. At the deck's long-run benchmark, and with the realisation haircut that an Indonesian sub-bituminous producer requires, the modelled average selling price settles near the mid-forties in US dollars a tonne against an all-in cash cost in the low thirties, a margin that is positive but far thinner than the last two reported years [S0, S6]. Discounted at the cost of equity and with no terminal value, that stream supports Rp4,191 a share, and the terminal value share of the total is 0.0% — which is the point of the method, since the entire value is explicit and none of it is a terminal assumption [S0].

The two cross-checks now part company with each other, and honesty requires us to say so rather than to average the disagreement away. The EV/EBITDA cross-check capitalises a normalised EBITDA at 6.4x times — the median of an explicit seaborne-export peer cohort (ADRO, AADI, BSSR, ITMG, PTBA, GEMS, MCOL, INDY), not BYAN's own peak-distorted four-year mean, which was struck when EBITDA was small in the price-war and low-volume years and is shown as the distribution it is in the table, not used as the anchor — and produces Rp3,946 a share, -5.9% versus the primary: the two methods now broadly agree, each capitalising the same forward cash flows. On the basis of the cross-check, one disclosure: the cohort median of 6.4x is the median of the eight-name seaborne set above [S0]; the four names under our own coverage whose latest-year multiples we can see print a lower median, so if the cross-check were struck on that narrower, house-covered subset alone it would land closer to the primary DCF rather than further from it — the cross-check is if anything generous to the share price, not to our target. The dividend-yield cross-check is the outlier. It capitalises the model's own forecast next-twelve-months payout at the cohort's median yield of 8.3%, producing Rp6,606, or 57.6% above the primary [S0]. It uses the model's payout on modelled earnings — which fall as the price normalises — so it is not the pre-cut stream, but capitalising any maintained dividend at a through-cycle yield still reaches a level the depleting reserve cannot fund. In plain terms: our primary method values the coal and the multiple cross-check agrees with it, while the dividend anchor values what the export complex will pay for this class of equity [S0].

None of the three methods reaches the price, and the ordering between them is itself the finding. The reserve DCF and the exit-multiple cross-check now broadly agree, because both capitalise the same forward cash flows; the dividend-yield anchor, which capitalises a payout the depleting reserve cannot fund, sits materially higher and is the only one of the three within reach of the tape [S0]. So the price is not being set by the coal at all — it is being set by the dividend, and the dividend is a function of the benchmark the market assumes persists. If the benchmark normalises toward the deck's long-run path and the payout is maintained, the DCF and the multiple cross-check will look right and the dividend anchor will collapse; if the premium persists indefinitely, the dividend anchor is still short of today's price and the shares are capitalising something none of our methods can see [S0, S6]. Which anchor you believe is the whole investment question, and we take the through-cycle view that the method card prescribes [S0].

The sensitivity grid shows the answer is almost entirely a benchmark question rather than a cost or volume question: a full deck-step change in the price assumption moves the value sharply while the volume and cost-intensity axes move it far less [S0]. One caveat on the exhibit: the IDR/USD axis is inert because Bayan reports and sells in US dollars, so the engine's translation of a USD cash-flow stream back to rupiah takes currency outside the sensitivity — the flat rows are a statement about the functional currency, not evidence that currency does not matter, and we discuss the two-sided translation risk in section five [S0, S8]. That price-taker profile with a fixed cost base is why we spend more of this report on the price deck than on the operating plan [S0].

Before we strike the value we re-checked the balance-sheet date. The last reported balance sheet is 30 June 2026, and nothing after it requires an adjustment to enterprise value: the second-quarter update showed cash of US$954.1m with no net debt and the capex programme intact [S8]; three subsidiaries declared force majeure in September pending the unapproved RKAB revision, after which extra quota was granted [S13, S14]; and the October control-block transfers were made between existing holders, so no cash reached the company [S2, S10]. No divestment, acquisition, special or interim dividend, rights issue, contingent consideration or asset held for sale was disclosed after that date, so the bridge stays empty and the value is struck on the reserve and the contracted book alone [S8, S13].

Finally, the reverse-DCF frame, which asks what the market price implies rather than what we think the price should be. The engine solves it on the nearest fully-market deck year, FY2027E (US$118/t a tonne), so the factor is stated against that marker and not the long-run one: holding our cost and volume assumptions, the current price of Rp10,475 requires the benchmark to average roughly 191 through the forecast horizon, about 1.6 times the deck's FY2027E marker and a larger multiple of the US$105/t long-run marker [S0]. That is above the current spot benchmark, which already embeds a war premium, and it is a demanding assumption to underwrite for a depleting asset [S0]. Note also that the deck's own near-year marker already sits below today's tape, so the required benchmark is above the deck outright rather than merely above a depressed long-run assumption [S0]. Either the premium persists indefinitely, or the shares are capitalising a dividend that a normalising price will not sustain [S0, S8]. We do not think both can be true.
The konglo lens: what the price is, and how much of the premium the regime keeps

Bayan is a konglo name — the listed vehicle of Low Tuck Kwong's group and a member of the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list — so the engine does not converge the value to the tape immediately. It measures the gap between the price and the fundamental value and, over the regime deck's own twelve-month scenarios, keeps a probability-weighted share of it. Today the tape is 2.4x the fundamental value: a premium, not a discount, and about as wide a gap as the lens prices [S19, S17]. The flags on the name — HSC membership, exclusion from the IHSG and the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80, deletion from the MSCI indexes, with no passive buyer left — are exactly the ones that raise the share of the log gap the regime closes rather than lower it [S19, S17].

The lens prices three regime paths that are independent of our business scenarios. The base path, the most likely, closes a little over a third of the log gap over the year and lands the target at Rp7,552 — still well below the tape. The bear path, the de-rating running at a second shock-year pace as it would under the MSCI Standalone decision or a wider enforcement wave, closes three-quarters of the gap and takes the value to Rp5,313 [S17]. The bull path, a relief rally that re-expands part of the gap rather than closing it, takes the value to Rp11,218. Our twelve-month target is the probability-weighted result, Rp7,909, set against a fundamental value of Rp4,265 — the price the most likely path still pays for a premium the cash flows do not justify.

Two features of this register keep the premium from closing faster, and between them they are why we are at REDUCE rather than at the outright negative the fundamental gap alone would suggest. First, the float is thin: the free float is 21.3% of the register against a minimum of fifteen percent, the control block is concentrated, and no holder is forced to sell — a concentrated register can stay expensive for far longer than a valuation-based seller can stay patient [S19, S18]. Second, the pending change of control is a dated event that can set a floor, and we now price it rather than only name it. A completed transfer of the control block to PT Jhonlin Baratama would trigger a mandatory tender offer under POJK 9/2018 struck at the higher of the deal price (2,588) and the prior-ninety-day market reference — and with the shares changing hands off-market at 2,588 on the 15 October transfer against a 11,100 close that day and an on-market purchase at 11,200 a day earlier, the ninety-day reference sits ABOVE today's Rp10,475 close, so a completed tender would floor the exit above our Rp7,909 target. That is a genuine asymmetry against the short, and we hold it as a dated, probabilistic catalyst rather than the base: the trigger is completion, and the company states plainly that no change of control has occurred — Low Tuck Kwong and Elaine Low still hold 30.3% together, marginally above Jhonlin's 30.2%, and the company has received no POJK 9/2018 takeover announcement [S10]. If the conditions precedent fail, the same event is a governance overhang that raises the required return — which is the bear. Neither feature makes the premium value; both decide how slowly it decays, and the tender is the one path on which the premium does not decay at all, which is why the bull regime keeps it.

The dominant downside risk is the coal price itself, and it is not a hypothetical. The deck's long-run benchmark is well below the current spot, which means our base case already assumes a substantial decline, and a faster or deeper normalisation would take the shares through our bear value in a single year [S0]. The mechanism is mechanical rather than subtle: a lower benchmark lowers the realised price, compresses the margin against a largely fixed cost base, and cuts the dividend, and the dividend is what the market has been paying for [S8].

The second risk is regulatory and it is specific to Indonesia. The RKAB approval regime gates production legally, and the current year showed that a delay is not a theoretical risk but a live one: three subsidiaries declared force majeure to their customers because they could not produce legally pending an approval [S13]. A repeat, or a lengthening of the approval cycle, hits volume and revenue directly and is outside management's control [S13]. The 2025 royalty regulations are the companion risk on the cost side, since a move into the stepped schedule would raise the cost line for producers in the converted-licence regime; the bear now carries that uplift explicitly, with the effective royalty stepping toward the top IUP rate the annual report quotes [S0, S6, F30]. The same regime can also lift the domestic-market share above the 25.7% we observe — the government is gating total output through RKAB rather than the DMO percentage, so we hold the capped share at its last actual, but a rising obligation would dilute realisation faster than the model allows and is a risk we watch [S6, F10].

The third risk is execution on capacity, though we regard it as the mildest. The barge-loading and camp programme is internally funded and the company has delivered on similar projects before, so the risk is slippage rather than failure [S6, S8]. Currency is a two-sided risk: the group reports in dollars and sells in dollars, so translation risk is limited, but a materially weaker rupiah would raise dollar costs over time even as it flatters reported margins briefly [S0, S8]. Liquidity is a real consideration for an outside investor rather than a fundamental one: the free float is 21.3% of the register, and the controlling block is concentrated, so the shares are liquid only by the standards of a large-cap, not of an index heavyweight [S0].

The fourth risk is governance, and it is the one we carry in the bear rather than leave in the narrative. A control-register transfer at a price far below the market, between parties connected with control, is the kind of event that can hold a trust discount on the register for as long as the ownership is unsettled — the reverse-DCF shows what that costs if the required return rises, and the model encodes it as a higher cost of equity rather than a price shock because a governance overhang changes the discount rate an outside holder demands, not the coal price: the base case carries a small overlay and the bear doubles it [S2, S10].

Thermal-coal producers are exposed to the same broad risks everywhere: price, permitting, cost
inflation and the energy transition. What differs by jurisdiction is who bears the permitting risk
and how the domestic-supply obligation is priced. In Indonesia the state carries the permitting
lever directly, which makes the policy calendar as important to a forecast as the price calendar.

Our scenario weights are 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull, close to symmetric because we see the two tails as genuinely balanced rather than as a skew to protect, and the tails now move the same four drivers (benchmark, volume, required return and royalty) by MIRRORED amounts — the volume shocks are the mirror pair, a clip and an equal step up, as the method card prescribes, now that the base itself runs at the company's stated ramp capacity. The bear is built from four parts, not the price alone, and its 25% weight reflects that all four must coincide. First, the benchmark is taken down a fifth from the deck's through-cycle path — the exact mirror of the bull's step up — which carries it through the marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names [S0]. Second, the RKAB squeeze persists and clips a twentieth of group volume: the September force-majeure declaration by the three subsidiaries [S13] was met by an additional 15 to 20 Mt of 2026 quota the government granted them [S14], so we carry a lasting group-level clip rather than the one-off event's full size, while the unchanged payout cuts the dividend mechanically with the lower price [S13, S14]. Third, the royalty regime tightens: the bear carries the IUP/CCoW-conversion risk with the effective royalty stepping up toward the top IUP rate, the schedule the annual report itself quotes [S6, F30]. Fourth, the ownership overhang is carried as a separate governance shock — a higher required return on the register, not a price move — which is how the Jhonlin block shows up in the bear rather than being left out of it [S2, S10]. We keep the bear at 25% rather than lift it: the reserve consumption and the force-majeure cure that would otherwise argue for a heavier downside are now IN the base — the reserve is netted and the base volume already carries the plan — so the tail is reserved for the genuinely uncertain conjunction of a price trough, a lasting quota clip, a royalty step-up and a governance re-rating arriving together [S6, S14]. Together the bear takes the value to Rp1,951 [S13]. The bull case mirrors each step: the premium holds and supply discipline lasts into the following year, so the benchmark runs a fifth above the deck's path; the royalty regime is eased rather than tightened; volumes run a twentieth above the base plan, which already sits at Bayan's low-cost 80 million-tonne ramp capacity funded by the US$770.0m already spent [S6, F33, F34]; and the ownership overhang settling removes the base's 1.0% governance charge from the required return and prices the register below the industry beta as the control question resolves — the exact mirror of the bear's charge, sourced to the same POJK 9/2018 control question [S10] — taking the value to Rp6,199 [S0, S8].
The konglo regime: the premium and its dated catalysts

The business scenarios above are only half the risk. The other half is the concentrated-ownership regime, which prices the name independently of the coal. On a konglo name the events the tape treats as noise — an index decision, a free-float deadline, an enforcement action — are flow events with no passive buyer on the other side, and they move what the market will pay for the same cash flows [S19, S17]. We carry three dated regime catalysts. First, the exchange's minimum-free-float rule steps up for the largest names in March 2027; Bayan is compliant on the disclosure we can see, so this is a flow risk for the class rather than a forced sale for Bayan, but it keeps a concentrated register the subject of the market's attention [S18]. Second, MSCI closes the feedback window on Indonesia's reclassification to Standalone status in April 2027 and decides by the end of June 2027; a Standalone outcome would put the HSC names outside the index universe entirely, and we hold that in the bear regime rather than the base [S17]. Third, the pending change of control and the tender offer that would follow completion are a dated price event in either direction — a regulator-set floor if it completes, a governance overhang if the conditions precedent are not met [S2, S10].

The two scenario sets relate deliberately: the business scenarios move the fundamentals the lens starts from, and the konglo regime scenarios decide how much of the price-to-value gap survives the year. A weak coal year and an aggressive regime can arrive together, which is the bear, but they are separate bets, and a reader should be able to see each one on its own [S19].

The signposts we will watch are concrete. A sustained move in the benchmark toward the deck's long-run path would validate the primary method and cut the value sharply; a breakdown in the RKAB approval discipline, or a repeat force majeure, would hit volume before it hit price; and any change to the royalty regime would move the cost line in a way the model would have to reflect [S0, S13]. On the other side, a decision by the board to maintain or raise the payout ratio through a price decline would be the strongest possible signal that management sees the downturn as cyclical rather than structural [S8].
The konglo profile

Bayan is a single-name group: the listed vehicle of Low Tuck Kwong, whose register is dominated by the founder and his family and, since the October transfers, by PT Jhonlin Baratama. It sits on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, which takes it out of the IHSG calculation and out of the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80, and it has been deleted from the MSCI indexes under MSCI's HSC treatment; HSC membership is a concentration reading and not a finding of wrongdoing [S19, S17]. The free float is 21.3% of the register, above the new fifteen-percent minimum, so Bayan is not a name facing a forced sell-down to comply — the flow risk for the class is real, but for Bayan the binding constraint is that so few shares trade that the marginal price is set by a thin market rather than by value [S19, S18]. The group's role is uncomplicated: Bayan is the flagship asset and the group's principal cash generator, and the corporate action that matters is the pending change of control — a conditional share purchase agreement, the PJBS the exchange referred to, which would transfer the control block to PT Jhonlin Baratama subject to conditions precedent, with the tender-offer obligation the takeover rules attach to completion [S2, S10].

Ownership and control are the governance story here, and they moved in the covered period — but the distinction that matters, and that the group registry records as 'pending' (as the red team notes), is between the SHARES having moved and CONTROL having changed. The shares moved: PT Jhonlin Baratama, which held nothing in the March 2026 shareholder list, held 30.2% of the issued and paid-up capital by the 19 October ownership report, while Dato' Low Tuck Kwong's stake fell to 8.3% [S5, S10]. Control did not: Dato' Low Tuck Kwong and Elaine Low still hold 30.3% together, marginally above Jhonlin's 30.2%, and the company states, on the basis of their 8 October 2026 control letters and the absence of any takeover announcement under POJK 9/2018, that it has received nothing showing a change of control [S10]. The 16 September 2026 conditional SPA is the agreed mechanism and the block transferred on its formula, but the formal change of control — and with it the mandatory tender offer — has NOT been triggered. That is the consistent reading of the disclosure: the 30.2% holding, the exchange's clarification questions and the registry's 'not yet completed' status all describe a block that has moved without control having passed.

The disclosed transfers that prompted the exchange's questions were executed off-market at Rp2,588 a share in the middle of that October and again at Rp2,588 a share the next day, against a Rp11,100 close on the first of those days and a Rp11,200 on-market purchase by Dato' Low Tuck Kwong the day before — so the transfer price is a little under a quarter of the tape, not a "small fraction" of it [S2, S10]. Two facts discipline the reading. First, the price is contractual rather than a discovery: the exchange tied the identical first-day price directly to the pelaksanaan Perjanjian Jual Beli Saham Bersyarat (PJBS), a conditional share purchase agreement, with Jhonlin Baratama, and asked whether a change to that agreement had produced a further transfer [S2]. The buyer is PT Jhonlin Baratama and the sellers are the control-block holders, so this is a transfer between connected parties on a PJBS formula, not a minority price fixed by the market [S10]. Second, the holdings confirm it moved between existing holders rather than off the register: as at the October ownership report Dato' Low Tuck Kwong held 8.3% of the capital, he and Elaine Low together held 30.3%, and PT Jhonlin Baratama held 30.2% as the resulting stake [S2, S10]. We therefore do not claim an unsourced aggregate block; the disclosure supports the per-date prices and the resulting holdings, and no more. The company answered that it was not a party to the transactions and could not confirm their substance, and both it and the ministry denied any link to the RKAB process [S2, S10, S15].

The question this raises for an outside shareholder is about the alignment of the controlling block rather than about disclosure compliance. A transfer at a price far below the market, from or to parties connected with control, is the kind of event that makes the market ask what the transacting parties believe the shares are worth, and it coincided with the RKAB approval process, which the mining ministry publicly stressed was unrelated to the share acquisition [S15]. We note that both the company and the ministry took the trouble to deny a connection, which tells you the connection was being made [S13, S15].

On the rest of the governance file the picture is unremarkable and mostly positive. The dividend record is strong and consistent, with a five-year average payout of 73.0% and a large distribution in respect of the last completed year [S8]. The board and audit arrangements show no flagged issues in the covered filings, there is no auditor downgrade or qualified opinion, and we found no serial equity issuance or pledge disclosure that would impair control [S6]. Related-party revenue is DISCLOSED AND QUANTIFIED, not dismissed: the group's coal revenue includes US$185.9m from related parties in the last full year — a low-single-digit share of group sales — against a larger related-party balance-sheet footing of US$35.2m trade payables and US$12.3m trade receivables, plus a US$51.9m civil-works contract with PT Nirmala Matranusa [S6]. That is the flag the methodology requires us to quantify, and we classify it optics-class rather than manipulation-class: the flows are disclosed line by line, small against revenue and assets, and the coal is also sold to third parties — but the payable is not nothing, and it sits beside the off-market block transfer above rather than being waved away [S6].

On ESG, the exposures are the ones intrinsic to thermal coal. The group's emissions are scope one and scope two from mining, hauling and barging plus the much larger scope three from combustion of the coal it sells, and the latter is the material figure for any investor applying a transition lens [S6]. Land rehabilitation and mine-closure obligations are a real long-tail liability for any Kalimantan producer, and the group's reclamation provisioning is a line we will track through the filings [S6]. On the social side, the mining workforce is large and locally concentrated, which creates both licence-to-operate value and community-relations risk [S6]. None of this changes the investment case at the price in question, but a transition-aware buyer should size the position for the scope-three exposure rather than for the reported emissions [S6].

The nearest catalyst is the operating update for the current quarter, which will show whether the force-majeure episode cost volume that the additional quota does not recover, and whether the contracted book of 67.2 Mt is holding [S8, S13]. Alongside it sits the FY2027 RKAB cycle for the three affected subsidiaries, because an orderly approval would remove the single largest operational tail risk in the model and a repeat delay would reprice it [S13].

The dividend decision is the value catalyst, and it is the one the market actually trades. The company's five-year record of a 73.0% payout is the anchor the multiple rests on, and a board decision to maintain or raise the payout through a weakening price would be read as a signal about management's own view of the cycle [S8]. Conversely, a cut would validate the primary valuation method faster than any price move [S0].

We will monitor a short list of indicators between updates. First, the benchmark price path against the deck's assumption, since the sensitivity grid shows it dominates every other variable [S0]. Second, the realised-price spread to the benchmark, because it is the company-specific number that tells us whether the quality discount is widening or narrowing [S6]. Third, unit cash costs against our bottom-up build, with fuel and contracting rates the inputs to watch [S8]. Fourth, the RKAB calendar and any further force-majeure disclosure [S13]. Fifth, and at the governance level, any further disclosure on the Jhonlin Baratama block and the resolution of the exchange's clarification request [S2, S10]. We will revisit the through-cycle marker itself if the complex moves, as the method card requires, rather than assuming the deck stands still [S0].

The regime calendar is now a monitored list in its own right, because on this name it sets the price as much as the coal does [S19]. The first dated item is the exchange's minimum-free-float step for the largest names at the end of March 2027 [S18]. The second is MSCI's Standalone decision, with the feedback window closing at the end of April 2027 and the decision due by the end of June 2027 [S17]. The third is any completion, amendment or lapse of the Jhonlin Baratama agreement and the tender-offer process that follows it, and any further exchange or regulator clarification on the October transfers [S2, S10]. We will also track the HSC list itself, since an addition or removal changes whether the lens carries the HSC flag at all, and with it the share of the premium the most likely path keeps [S19].

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds and overshoots: the bear takes the deck's long-run Newcastle marker down a full 20% (the exact mirror of the bull, the house default), which is a demand-led trough through the US$100-110/t marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names, and the RKAB quota squeeze persists and clips a twentieth of group volume — the disclosed one-off cure ESDM granted the three affected subsidiaries was larger, an additional 15-20 Mt or about a fifth to a quarter of group output [S14], so the bear carries a lasting residual clip rather than the temporary halt annualised. On the cost side the IUP/CCOW conversion risk crystallises and the effective royalty steps up toward the top IUP rate — a +3.5pp move on the royalty line. The new Jhonlin control block is carried as a separate +200bp governance overhang on the required return rather than as a price move, and the lower benchmark with the unchanged 73% payout cuts the dividend mechanically — so the bear value and the dividend cut arrive together, because the dividend is the anchor the market pays for.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same four drivers: the war premium holds and Chinese mine-safety curbs plus RKAB discipline keep seaborne supply tight into 2027, so the benchmark runs 20% above the deck's long-run path; Bayan's low-cost Tabang tonnes take share and volumes run 5% above the base plan as the Muara Pahu and Tabang capacity, funded by the US$0.77bn of debottlenecking capex already spent, runs full — with the base already at the company's more-than-80-million-MT-per-annum ramp target [S6, F33], the bullish volume leg is the mirror of the bear's clip rather than a second step up; the royalty regime is eased rather than tightened; and as the ownership overhang settles the required return falls 200bp rather than rises (round-1 review C10). The mechanism is the reverse of the base case's own overlay: the base carries a +100bp governance charge on the required return for the live exchange clarification over the off-market control-block transfer [S2, S10], and the bull removes that +100bp and prices the register 100bp below the industry beta as the control question is resolved — whether the Jhonlin process completes into a tender or lapses, either outcome ends the POJK 9/2018 uncertainty the company itself flagged in its 23 Oct 2026 disclosure [S10]. The -200bp is thus the exact mirror of the bear's +200bp (which is the base +100bp doubled), sourced to the same governance event the base prices.
